lesson.subtitle: Lesson 20 -- If the Tourists Keep Coming
lesson.title_tag: Professor View -- Ricardo Wertheim | Lesson 20 -- If the Tourists Keep Coming
lesson.grammar_point: first conditional for real future possibilities (if plus present simple, will or won't plus verb)

vocab.title: Match each word to its meaning
defs: to leave the house or apartment where you live and go to live in another place
quiet and calm, with no noise or stress
with too many people in one place
to say that only a certain number is allowed, and no more
the money you pay every month to live in a house or apartment that is not yours
a very big boat where people sleep, eat and travel for days on holiday
to keep someone or something safe from danger or damage
a store that sells small things that tourists take home

paras: Dubrovnik is a small city with a big problem. Only about forty thousand people live there, but more than a million visitors arrive every year. On a busy day in August, several cruise ships stop near the old town in the morning, and by ten o'clock the main street is overcrowded. You cannot walk, you cannot stop, and you cannot see the stones under your feet.

The people who live inside the old walls feel it most. Many apartments are now rented to tourists, so the rent is very high for local families. Many of them have moved out, and today fewer than two thousand people live in the old town. A woman who grew up there says: "If the last families leave, the old town will become a museum. It will be beautiful, but it won't be alive."

So the city decided to act. It now limits the number of cruise ships that can stop each day, and it asks visitors to respect the people who live there. The message to travelers is simple: if you come in spring or autumn, you will find a peaceful city. And if the visitors help, the city will protect its old town for the next generation.

bank.label: Useful sentences for possible results
items: If more ships come, the streets will be overcrowded.
If the rent goes up, young families will move out.
If you come in May, you will find a peaceful city.
If we leave early, we will avoid the crowds.
If the city doesn't act, the old town will become a museum.
What will happen if the families leave?
I won't go in August if I can choose.

listenings.text: Hello, Ricardo! It's Elena, from the guesthouse in Dubrovnik. You asked me about next year, so here is my advice. If you come in August again, you will see the city at its busiest. There will be cruise ships near the harbor and long lines at the city walls. But if you come in May or in October, you will find a different city. The streets will be peaceful, the sea will still be warm, and you will have the old town almost for yourself. And one more thing. If you stay inside the walls, you will meet the families who still live here. There are not many of us now. If you tell me your dates soon, I will keep your old room for you.

My family has lived inside these walls for four generations. When I was a boy, about five thousand people lived in the old town. Now there are fewer than two thousand. My neighbors moved out, one by one, because the rent was too high. If this continues, my children won't live here. But please understand, I am not against tourists. They are good for the city, and my little cafe needs them. The new rules help a lot: fewer cruise ships, and more visitors in spring and autumn. If the city protects the old town, and the visitors respect it, we will all win. If not, in twenty years there will be nobody here to sell you a coffee.

extra_audio.text: First Ricardo and Elena walked into the old town at ten in the morning. Then they saw three cruise ships near the harbor. After that the main street was so overcrowded that they could not walk. Then Elena said that her neighbors moved out because the rent was too high. Next they climbed to a quiet street behind the walls. In the end Ricardo said: If I come back in May, I will stay here.
